text: The power op can report failure on a target tile that a pole doesn't need to cover itself (e.g. a spot between machines), so aim each power step at an actual consumer (an inserter or machine edge) and do one per far-apart consumer. Don't hand-place isolated poles and assume they connect.

For long-distance outposts (>~120 tiles), split every belt and pole run into legs of ≤~100 tiles, and start each pole leg from a pole you have verified is on the target grid (find its exact position first). Don't count the item supply only at the start: check that the total pole count covers the whole distance (distance/8 plus extras), and stock up before leaving.

To feed a machine from an existing belt, place the machine and its input inserter right beside that belt, rather than extending or branching a new belt off it. If the checker says a connect start is mid-line, don't force it from a neighbouring tile: the new belt won't be fed.

The power op can report "still unpowered" even after its poles connect the grid, so check the area before retrying power steps and don't treat that error alone as a failure. Power every inserter and assembler in one pass by placing poles explicitly so each 5x5 area covers them, including output inserters on the far side of a machine.

On a shared product belt, every producer must drop its item upstream of every consumer's pickup point, and each item needs its own lane. Check the belt's flow direction against each drop and pickup tile before building; never fix a belt by rotating it while it still holds items, rebuild it empty instead.

A small pole only powers 2 tiles each side of itself, so check that every inserter, not just the assemblers, falls inside some pole's 5x5 area; inserters at the edge of a row of machines are the usual gap. If one machine in a row of identical ones is starved while its belt is full, check the inserter's power first, before waiting or rebuilding.

For a long power run, lay medium poles yourself in one straight line at a fixed spacing of 7–8 tiles, from a pole you have confirmed is on the grid. Where line segments join, check that no hop is longer than 9 tiles, because one hop just past reach leaves the whole outpost on a dead grid. Belt transit is slow, so wait about 1 second per 2 belt tiles before checking delivery, and check that drills

Check each tech's unlock type before queueing it, because some techs (like oil-processing) unlock by a trigger, not by lab research. If a ghost is left unbuilt, build it where it stands with build_ghosts aimed right at it, and move the character off the footprint first; never place a real entity on top of it.

Before choosing a machine's footprint, check the area for other characters, AFK players and items on the ground, because those block placement and can't be moved by moving yourself. If a placement is blocked by something you don't control, move the machine to clear ground right away instead of retrying the same spot.

Before planning to mine or rebuild existing belts, check who built them: player-built entities need force_pickup=true, and an order from ops to fix that system counts as permission, so pass it up front. Items lying on belts can't be taken with take, so clearing contamination means picking up those belts, not taking items off them.

Never reuse a spot a past plan found blocked by another character or items on the ground; choose fresh ground checked with free_space. Give each new machine supplies the actor can't pull back out: it fetches from any chest, so stocking a new chest can empty the input chest of a machine that is already running.

Science only counts when labs consume it, so any science order also needs a running research. Queue several candidate lab techs that use those packs in one plan, because already-researched ones are skipped and trigger techs fail, and check that the labs report research in progress before building production.

"Automated, no hand-feeding" means every ingredient reaches the target machines from other assemblers or a belt (e.g. a gear assembler and a plate feed belt), not from chests the character stocks by hand. Build that supply chain in the first plan, sized for the required rate (assembler-1 makes 6 red packs/min, so 15/min needs 3 of them).

When a player's check keeps reporting zero for something that looks built and working, stop guessing after one retry. Ask in chat exactly what the check counts, and trace every input back to a real source such as smelters or a belt, because chests the character stocks probably count as hand-feeding.

Ops' capacity check counts only assemblers fed entirely by inserters from a belt or another machine, with no input from chests. Work out the required machine count from 6 red packs per minute per assembler-1, and build all of them on one shared ingredient belt in the first plan.

When iron output is zero, trace the ore supply back to its source first, and keep any new feed belt short, built in legs with its end on a free tile that isn't next to another belt line (a half-built connect can merge into a foreign belt). If a step times out, check `me` for a stale running job and the character's position (stuck on belts or water) before resubmitting, and route moves around water

Before any fetch/take/craft step, check the character's free inventory slots; if it's nearly full (e.g. thousands of stone), first dump the bulk into a nearby chest or machine so takes don't fail with misleading "nothing to take" errors. Also look inside existing furnaces for fuel (coal) before concluding there's none on the map, and redistribute it instead of travelling far for wood.

When fuel is missing and find shows no coal on the map, look inside the fuel slots of furnaces and boilers that are already running (find doesn't list them). Take only part from each so every one keeps some, and work out per-furnace amounts from what you actually took, not from the stock you assumed, so the last furnaces still get fuel.

Size every inserter on a mall's supply path for throughput: a basic inserter moves only ~0.83 items/s while a gear assembler eats 2 plates/s, so use fast inserters for the depot-to-belt loader and the upstream gear feeder's in/out from the start. Otherwise the first machine starves everything downstream.

To tie a new build to an existing grid, find the grid pole's exact position and place your own medium pole bridge yourself, checking that every hop is no more than 9 tiles (the power op's small poles can land just past their 7.5-tile reach and leave a dead grid). Plan this bridge pole in the first ghost layout instead of relying on a power step.

The actor crafts on its own between steps, so check `me` for already-made items before any explicit take/craft step and skip the ones already covered. For a new mining field, place every pole explicitly so each drill sits in some pole's 5x5 area and every hop to a known grid pole is under 7.5 tiles. Also check that the boilers have coal, because a power op's success doesn't mean the drills are run

When the grid comes from an electric-energy-interface or a pole you were only told about, the power op may not count it as powered. So lay the connecting pole line yourself with explicit medium-pole place steps every 7–8 tiles from that pole's exact position (find it first), and keep the last hop to a small pole within 7.5 tiles.

The power op can't start from a pole fed only by an electric-energy-interface. So in the build plan itself, run the line from the given grid pole with explicit medium-pole place steps every ≤8 tiles, ending within 7.5 tiles of the build's first small pole. Once a build is powered, check its output before rebuilding, because ops' "0 made" report can be stale from before power came on.

Before scaling production, trace the existing line end to end: furnaces stopped on full output mean the plate belt has no sink, and boilers low on fuel mean power will die. Fix both first. Take bulk fuel only from a named storage chest with take, never with a generic fetch, and do every stocking insert last, because fetch pulls from the nearest chest and can empty the fuel chests you just filled.

When several consumers pick up from one belt that a producer drops onto, check every consumer's pickup tile lies downstream of the producer's drop tile in the belt's flow direction (place consumers past the drop, never beside the start of the belt). Also put fuel into every boiler at the start of any big build and make sure each one has an automatic coal feed, because the added load drains unfed b

Build right where the order points, inside the stretch of the source belts nearest the given coordinates, because ops' checks seem to count only machines and chests near those spots. Wire power yourself with explicit pole place steps from the named grid pole, since the power op may not treat an energy-interface grid as powered.

Before branching off or connecting to an existing belt, look at a small radius right at the tap point to confirm the line's real extent and end, because wide area views truncate lines. Then verify the tap actually got built (splitter placed, new belt fed) before building downstream. When two connect routes run next to a block's input/output belts, end each one on a tile that no other belt points i

For a long small-pole run, don't chain connect legs whose end is off-grid (connect errors and leaves hops just over 7.5 tiles where legs meet); place the poles yourself in one straight line at a fixed 6–7 tile spacing from a verified grid pole, or do one connect leg at a time and verify that its last pole is on the base grid before starting the next leg. Don't place a splitter on a belt that's already running with items, because placing it over existing belts can fail. To feed one machine, put its input inserter and the machine right beside the existing belt, on whichever side the player allows, and run only the output to a chest.

When a plan fails midway, the skipped steps often include power poles for things already built, so recheck every new inserter's power before calling a machine fixed. For a long pole run, connect legs often end with a hop just past 7.5 tiles where they meet, so after each leg check the next leg's start area for the grid id and bridge with an explicit pole placed within about 4 tiles of the last pow

When a player changes a job mid-plan, check the area once to see what was actually built, then submit one plan for the latest instruction only, rather than also re-answering the cancelled plan's failure report. If ops reserves a side of a belt, keep the machines and the power route off that side, and say plainly when the new spot moves away from the coordinates the order named.

When a chemical plant or refinery reports missing fluid, map its existing pipes with find pipe first, then check which side its inputs face and that each fluid reaches the input port the recipe assigns to it (first fluid ingredient on the first input box). Re-pipe or rotate to match, and check for poles in the pipe path, instead of adding a new water source.

Before scaling production, budget power and fuel first: add up the new load against generation that is actually fed (every boiler needs an inserter-fed coal supply, and a new steam block must be wired to the existing grid with explicitly placed poles that reach a generator or pole of that grid), and verify both before building consumers. Never put temporary feedstock in a chest the actor can fetch

Put chest-stocking inserts (and a bulk take from the named storage chest) early in a plan, right after the feeders are built, because the long steps at the end often don't run and a block built but never stocked counts as failed. When merging a new product belt into an existing one, end it with a side-load onto the free lane (approach from the side, never from behind the head) and check the lane e

A science order is measured by packs consumed, so in the same plan that builds a new pack line, move a tech that uses that pack to the front of the research queue (research with first=true); otherwise labs stuck on a tech that doesn't use the new pack report 0 used. Also clear any foreign items off a shared lab belt by picking up its whole tail past every lab inserter, not just the last few tiles.

Put a new production site's output belt on the same side of the base's parallel belt lines as its consumer (labs), or point its output toward open ground. Before building, check that the output end has a clear path: a belt facing a band of 3+ packed parallel belts can't cross them, because undergrounds span only 4 tiles.

On a belt that several producers drop onto, trace its flow direction tile by tile: every drop or side-load must land upstream of every consumer's pickup, and "north" means more negative y. When adding an inserter later, place a pole whose 5x5 area covers it in the same step, and leave a known free exit corridor for the output belt toward its consumer before building.

Mining drills have no recipe, so a "working" expect with recipe=<ore name> finds nothing; check a mine with belt_carries on its output belt and has_item at the destination chest (plus powered near the drills) instead. Before treating a failed expect as a real failure, look at the area: if the machines show "working" and items are arriving, fix the check, not the build.

For a multi-block science build, don't spread blocks apart and join them with many long crossing connect routes through splitter/merge manifolds: routes over ~40 tiles hit the search limit, and earlier lines box in later stubs. Place producers right next to their consumers so each feed is a short straight belt, give every manifold stub a reserved, open approach corridor, and route the most constra

Submitting a new plan (even a more=true part) replaces whatever plan is still running, so put every remaining step of a fix into one plan, ordered so that critical links (belts reaching consumers, fuel) come before optional expansion. Never place a block or chest where the character stands or in a pocket against water: put the character outside the footprint first, and check afterwards that it can

An upstream feeder machine (e.g. a gear assembler fed by a basic inserter) reports ingredient shortage for its first seconds while items travel, so put a wait of ~15-20 s at the end of the plan before the expect checks run. Before treating a "starved" expect as a failure, look at the area: if the machine now shows working, just re-verify instead of rebuilding.

An upgrade order is judged by whether the line still delivers, so before submitting, trace the line to its consumer and fix anything that stops the flow there, like an unpowered end inserter or a pole gap over 7.5 tiles that leaves part of the line on a dead grid. Do those fixes in the same plan, and check the rate at the destination chest, not just whether items are on the belt.

Don't add explicit take steps for items an upgrade or place step needs, because the actor already fetches them and a take fails when they're already in hand. If you do want a take, check `me` first and skip it when the inventory already holds the items.

Don't pass only=true to an upgrade step; only takes a list of entity names, and a bare true breaks the into lookup with a misleading "nothing upgrades into" error. For an area upgrade, give just into, x, y and a radius that covers every target, and leave only out unless you're listing names.

Ops' red science check wants about 30 packs/min even when the order only says "at least N assemblers", so size the build for 30/min from the start. That means 5+ assembling-machine-1 at 6/min each, or 4 assembling-machine-2 at 9/min each.

When a grid browns out, size new generation for the full peak load of every consumer once it's all running (assembler-2 150 kW each plus inserters, and treat any electric-energy-interface as a possible drain), not for the load you see while machines are stalled. Add at least 50% headroom: if the peak is over one boiler's 1.8 MW, build a second boiler with 2 engines in the first plan instead of jus

When placing poles by hand for a hand-laid layout, check every inserter's tile against each pole's supply area (medium covers center±3, small ±2), especially the one-tile gaps between machines midway between two poles. A single unpowered hand-off inserter starves the whole chain, so add a small pole in any gap the poles' areas don't reach.

A burner drill drops onto one specific tile in front of it, so any inserter tapping its output belt must pick from a tile at or downstream of that drop tile, never from the belt's head tile upstream of it. Check the drop tile with block_info or a close area look before placing the tap, or route a refuel chain from a tile that coal visibly passes.

When a long coal belt must reach a furnace column, lay its first tiles by hand away from other belts (go under any belt next to the drills explicitly), build the merge_lanes approach before the ore belt ever reaches the column so ore never sits on the coal lane, and give the plate output a sink (inserters into chests) at its end. Then wait at least belt length / 1.875 tiles/s before checking furna

Bus lanes come in pairs with two free columns between pairs, so a spare lane's x is not simply the next tile after the plate lanes; read its real position from the bus's lane list or the bus_in result before writing belt_carries checks on it. Put the check on a tile downstream of the merge that you know lies on that lane.

Before tapping a bus lane, check how much it really carries: a lane loaded by inserters from one side has only one belt lane full, about 7.5/s. A splitter hands only half of what passes to its tap while the bus end has a sink, so add up the iron every tap needs. If the lane can't cover that plus the sink's half, fill its empty belt lane at the bus head first, rather than adding more splitters.

A ghosts layout can't place a splitter over an existing belt, so to split a running belt by hand, put a mine_at step for that belt tile right before a place step for the splitter (outside the ghosts batch). Do this for every splitter that lands on an existing line.

When a row of machines needs only one item from a two-item plate belt (e.g. only cable needs copper, everything else iron), don't merge both taps onto one dead-end feed belt: the item consumed slowly fills both lanes and starves the others. Give the slow item its own short belt to its single consumer, or end the shared belt in a sink, and check that every leftover merge stub is removed so nothing

merge_lanes routes the two feed lines itself, so end each connect a few tiles short of the merge with open ground around the merge tile, and don't put that tile right next to where the lines end. Its "no route" error can come after the two side-loads are already built, so look at the merge tile before redoing it, then send only the steps after it.

When a project is already running and the same order comes back with player feedback, don't call start_project again. Pass the measured shortfalls to the running project or plan the next concrete fix. When first building a science line, leave free ground beside it and no return belt hugging its sides, so a later "double it" can just extend the row.

A connect or bus_in can't end on or pass through tiles a block's own pipes and belts use: end a fluid feed one tile outside the block's port tile, and route it around existing pipes of another fluid by hand (pipe lines in a ghosts step). End product lines at least 4 tiles east of the bus edge so bus_in has room for its own crossing, and read the tap's real end from its result before connecting fro

To feed a block's fluid port, don't end a plain connect on the tile just outside the port: use connect with to_fluid, or hand-place the last pipes (pipe-to-ground pairs past the block's edge so the new pipe never touches the block's other pipes). Place the block so a source pipe sits directly against its port when you can.

`clear line=` follows a belt through every merge and side-load into the whole connected network, so on tangled belts it also removes taps, splitters and bus lanes. Fix such tangles with mine_at on the few junction tiles, and don't reuse a bus row whose registered tap or merge you removed by hand: lay those lanes yourself with explicit belt lines instead of bus_in or tap.

Before merge_lanes or connect from tap ends, read each tap's real end tile from its result or a close area look (they're often a tile off from where you'd guess), and give the merge tile and the whole row path open ground well away from the tap belts. Never use clear line= on a feeder that already merges into the row belt: it takes the merged belt with it, so mine single tiles instead.

When a block's fluid port sits next to the block's own pipes or near a source pipe, don't rely on connect (it reports the port's neighbour as blocked): place the block so the source pipe is directly adjacent to the port, or lay the short feed pipe by hand as a ghosts pipe line onto the tile just outside the port, after a find pipe to see the block's internal pipes. Leave at least 6 free tiles between the bus edge and a block's two-lane input so merge_lanes has room, and right after the merge check that the block's first input belt tile carries both items; if not, find the real belt tiles with find transport-belt before rotating or mining anything. merge_lanes can leave a junction where one feed dead-ends into the other's underground entrance (find transport-belt doesn't list undergrounds, and rotating one flips it), so after a merge check that the block's first input tile carries BOTH items before building on. If one is missing, don't rotate tiles blindly: hand-lay a short ghosts belt that side-loads the missing item onto the free side of t

A row step needs its belt tile to already run across the side you give, and merge_lanes may leave its output running sideways or tangled with undergrounds. So for a furnace column off two bus taps, lay the merged feed yourself: ghost a straight belt running the way the row should go, side-load ore onto it from one side and connect coal into it from the other with end_direction (going under the bel

When two product lines must join into one two-lane belt for a row (e.g. iron + cable for circuits), don't use merge_lanes into a tight spot next to the feeding machines; lay the joint by hand in one ghosts step: a straight head belt with one tile behind it, the two feeds turning into its sides on the same tile from opposite directions, and the row's belt continuing straight on. To give ore and coal their own lanes on a furnace feed belt, feed each one in from opposite sides by hand: ore side-loads from one side, coal comes under the feed belt with an underground pair and side-loads from the other side. Never trust connect's end_direction or merge_lanes for this. Before the row step, check with an area look that the feed belt shows both items and that the joining lines en

merge_lanes reports no end and often leaves its belt running the wrong way, so to put two products on one belt for a row, hand-lay it in a ghosts step: a straight belt with at least one tile behind each side-load, one product side-loaded from each side. Feed any single feeder assembler (gears for a whole science row) with fast inserters in and out, because a basic inserter caps it near 25 gears/mi

After placing a built-in block, look at it closely before anything else: count its machines against the block's build list and look for inserters that pick from empty ground, because a block can come out missing a machine (e.g. one blocked by an existing pole line at its edge). When a block underperforms, check for missing machines before blaming supply, and keep blocks a few tiles clear of existi

Don't let merge_lanes or route build two-item lane merges at block inputs (they produced head-on and wrong-way belts every time); hand-lay each one as a ghosts layout: a stub belt behind the merge tile, one feed side-loading from each side, then straight belts into the block, and check both items reach the block's first tile before building the next block. When a block has two or more output belts and a feed belt on the same edge, lay all of them in ONE route step (from each output's port tile to its bus_in end, coal from the tap end to the input), with every bus_in end on its own row at least 8 rows apart, never as separate connects. A later connect boxes in or side-loads into an earlier line, which mixes products on a bus lane. Take each port tile

When a machine says an ingredient is "on its belt but not arriving fast enough", trace that feed line back to its source tap tile by tile before adding branches or machines, because an earlier repair often leaves a one-tile gap that cuts the supply. Fix the break first, and check the line carries the item just downstream of the source.

connect often slips an underground pair onto the very tile you planned to side-load into or feed from, so lay the last few tiles of every side-load, lane merge and block-output join by hand with ghosts (plain belts only) and route connect's end a few tiles away from them. Never assume which lane a tapped plate belt uses: side-load the plates onto a fresh belt from the side you want, and only then

Before building a consumer off a bus lane, add up every tap's draw on that lane (including bus-end sinks, and splitter taps that keep pulling while their consumer has room) against what the lane really carries, about 7.5/s if it's loaded from one side. If the total is over, fill the lane's empty belt-lane at the head with side-loading inserters in the SAME plan. Also check the second input (e.g. s

When extending a block's output belt, never lay a new belt line over an existing output tile: look at the exact tiles where the old output turns, then side-load the new line onto a straight stretch of it. Before judging a rate, check the bus end for sink chests, because a splitter tap only gets half while the bus end drains. Remove the sinks on lanes the new consumers need, then wait until the lan

Before planning a build, check with recipe that every machine it needs is unlocked (e.g. electric-mining-drill may not be), count steps exactly, because "end:N" uses the 1-based step number of the tap/row itself (a step inserted earlier shifts it), and put each feed belt on the tile directly west of the block's input tile from block_info, not one tile further out. A built-in block's input belts that dead-end inside it will spill onto any belt placed on the tile just past that end, so never route an output belt across the tile beyond an input belt's last tile; pass under it with an underground starting at the output port. Before adding consumers of an intermediate, run diagnose on it and on its own inputs (e.g. advanced circuits AND the electronic circuits feeding them) and size the upstream to cover total demand with ~20% headroom, since adding assemblers without more upstream supply just leaves them starved. Also cut a bus lane just below its last tap (or use no splitter), because a splitter tap passes half the f

Never feed a belt into the side of an underground belt entrance: items jam there and nothing passes, so always enter an underground from directly behind, with one straight belt tile before it pointing the same way. When items pile up just before a join, count them per tile to find the exact tile where they stop, and suspect a side-loaded underground or splitter there before re-laying belts that lo

When consumers starve while their producer makes more than they use, compare made vs used (production/diagnose) and follow the item's lane past every tap to find where the surplus actually goes, e.g. a bus lane that drains to the bus end, before rebuilding joins or adding machines. A bus lane cut by removing one belt tile gets bridged with an underground pair by later bus steps, so stop a lane per

Before repairing a broken tap or belt junction, look at it with a radius-2 area and trust the listed faults and tile kinds (an orphan underground exit can't be fed from behind; a 1-tile gap the fault names is the real break), then fix exactly those tiles with mine_at/place/rotate instead of re-routing with connect. Put belt_carries checks only on tiles the area listing shows are part of the line,

An ore patch's reported area is only a bounding box and its edges are ragged, and the point a player pins may sit on the rim. So place mining drills near the middle of that box (or look closely with a small-radius area at the exact drill spots), never within a few tiles of its edge.

For a multi-chain science order off a bus, build and verify one chain at a time (taps, then the intermediate assembler, then the hand-laid two-lane merge, then the science row, then bus_in), reading each step's real belt ends before designing the next, instead of one big plan that guesses tap and row end tiles. Check the rate at the science output before moving to the next chain.

To fill both lanes of a bus pair from one supply belt, feed only the first lane and then put a splitter across the pair a couple of rows below the bus head, instead of splitting the supply belt and running a second feed. The four feeds of two pairs crowd the bus head, so the last feed's start gets walled in.

When putting a pump into a long pipeline, don't end a connect right on the tile beside the pump (it reports that end tile as blocked). End each connect leg two tiles away from the pump and hand-place a pipe on each tile next to the pump's input and output.

When putting a pump into a long pipeline, hand-place one pipe on the tile right after the pump's output, then start the next connect from the tile after that pipe. A connect that starts on the tile touching the pump is refused as "start tile blocked", even though the tile is free.

Before feeding an intermediate assembler from one bus lane tap, compare the lane's real inflow (a single fast inserter source is only ~2.3/s split across lanes, and a splitter tap gets half while the bus end is still filling) with what the assembler needs. If it falls short, tap both lanes of that item from the start and join the second tap into the side of the first tap's belt.

A science line feeding labs is judged on a sustained rate, and labs on slow research use far fewer packs than the line makes, so the belt backs up and production drops. Always end the lab feed belt in an overflow inserter and chest past the last lab, and tap both lanes of a one-side-loaded plate item for any intermediate that needs more than half of one lane.

Before laying a fluid feed pipe beside a built-in block, find the block's own pipes and keep every new plain pipe off tiles touching a pipe of another fluid (use pipe-to-ground pairs past them, or place the block so the source sits on its port). If fluids do mix, flush the whole contaminated segment, including the block's own pipe-to-ground pairs, by mining and re-placing every piece in it, not ju

A rate check on a new oil build fails if it's measured right after building, because the refineries and pipes need a minute or two to fill and the output belts to start flowing. End such plans with a wait of 90-120 s before the rate check, and use working checks for the parts that don't have a rate target.

When routing a product line back for bus_in, end it at least 4 tiles east of the bus's outermost lane, spare lanes included (each pair has two free columns between pairs, so the outer edge is further out than the plate lanes). Ending it closer makes bus_in fail as blocked by its own last belt.

The supply step can merge two bus taps by feeding both into one tile that then side-loads onto the block's input belt, which mixes the items onto a single lane and starves the block. Right after supply, look closely at the block's first input tile and check that each item side-loads from its own side (one from each side, never both through the same joining tile) before judging a rate or checking t

When a build puts its product back onto a bus lane that nothing consumes yet, end that lane in a sink (a fast inserter into a chest at the bus end) in the same plan, or the lane backs up and the producers stop within minutes. Also check right after supply that the block's two-item input belt really has each item on its own lane (one side-loaded from each side), since a shared joining tile mixes th

Before tapping a bus plate lane twice for one build, check its head: if inserters load it from one side it carries only ~7.5/s and a downstream splitter tap gets half of what's left while the bus end still fills, so in the same plan side-load the lane's empty belt-lane at the head (a fast inserter from a source chest onto a stub belt that side-loads from the free side). Then judge a new block's ra

Before tapping a bus lane near its end, look at the bus end for sink inserters into chests and remove the sink on every lane the new consumer taps in the same plan. A sink drains the lane without limit, so a splitter tap gets only half the flow and starves a whole block even when the bus head is fully fed.

Before building a consumer of an intermediate made upstream (e.g. advanced circuits for purple science), run diagnose on it and check its producers actually run at full rate; a block fed by a second splitter tap on a draining bus lane (or a single long-handed inserter) gets only a quarter of the lane, so cut that lane just below its last tap and feed block ports with a belt, in the same plan. A new consumer on a splitter tap of a bus lane only gets about half the lane's leftover flow until the lane below the tap has backed up to the bus end, which takes minutes on a long bus. So end every new-tap build's plan with a wait of 5-7 minutes before its working/rate checks, or cut the lane just below the last tap when nothing downstream needs it.

Infinity chests used as bus-end sinks delete what they receive (they always show "holds nothing"), so never try to pull a lane's items back out of one. To feed a consumer from a lane's end, remove that lane's sink inserter and chest and run the lane's belt straight on into the consumer's feed.

Then join each block's output to its next con

Before a bus_in, look at the bus's side with a small area check over the rows from the merge row to the bus end. bus_in needs its incoming line's last belt to sit in open ground clear of the bus's tap belts and undergrounds. If taps surface near that row, route the product line to a free tile at least two columns off the bus side (or pick a bus_in row clear of tap exits) before calling bus_in.

When an order names a rate a little above what one built-in block gives (like 45/min green science against green-science-6's 30/min), place that one block, then upgrade its assemblers to assembling-machine-2 (speed 0.75 against 0.5 gives exactly 1.5x). Size its feeds and circuit supply for the higher rate, and check it with a rate check, rather than hand-building a bigger custom layout.

An order that chains several builds (circuits, then green science, then a bus_in, then labs off new taps, then a research queue) should go to start_project, or be submitted as parts with more=true. Make the first part only the taps plus the circuit build, checked with a working check, and add each later build on top of verified output instead of putting everything in one plan.

Before placing blocks in a bounded area, add up every block's footprint from block_info (plus a few tiles for taps, merges and feed belts) and check it fits with free_space. If the main block nearly fills the space alone, put its gear and circuit blocks outside it on open ground next to the bus, rather than crowding them in and blocking the main block's input tiles.

For green science off a bus, build the built-in blocks: electronic-circuit-3-2 (or gear-circuit-block) and green-science-6 placed with block steps, fed with supply steps off the bus. Don't hand-design the gear, cable, circuit, inserter and belt assemblers. Link each block's output to the next block's input with a short hand-laid ghosts belt, then bus_in the packs from open ground clear of tap exit

When an order repeats a build that failed before, first look over the target area and the bus taps with an area check, and clear every leftover from the earlier tries (half-built blocks, stub belts, splitters, ghosts, stray poles) with targeted clear or mine_at steps. Only then lay the new build, because old stubs and ghosts take the tiles the new block's inputs, taps and bus_in need.

When an order names a bounded patch of free ground, compare each block's footprint at every rotation with block_info and free_space before choosing a layout. A green-science-6 (23x13) plus a circuit block won't fit a 15x18 patch. When a player asks for something the character can't do (drive vehicles, fight) but also hints at a goal like taking new land, say so and in the same reply ask them to ping the spot, then check the pinged area before answering. A pinged spot already inside the base's power lines with no ore or biters isn't new land, so name what's actually there and offer concrete builds instead of guessing.

When covering an ore patch with drills, put a medium pole within 3 tiles of every drill's edge, including the outermost columns, and leave a 1-tile walking lane every few drill rows. Stop the layout a column short of patch edges that border lava, water or cliffs: drills packed edge to edge wall the character out, and later pole, mine or build steps there fail with "no path".

When build_ghosts builds nothing ("ghosts I couldn't build") or a place fails with "no path", first test a one-tile move. If even that reports "stuck", the character itself is trapped, so the plan has to free it first (mine whatever is around it, or use a roboport with construction bots for the work) instead of retrying the same builds from new standing spots.

Water, cliffs or dense buildings around a guessed point make the move fail with "no path" before anything gets built.

In an old mining field packed with drills, belts and poles, don't plan moves to tiles inside it: first test that the character can walk there (area look for walkable lanes, or a short move), and if it's walled in, mine a path in from the outside edge or start the work from the field's open edge. Pick up stopped drills from the outer edge inwards so every later step has a path.
